source_text: At enim ut malum postea erupit atque inde iam coepit bonitas dei cum aduersario agere, aliud quoque negotium eadem illa iustitia dei nacta est, iam secundum aduersationem dirigendae bonitatis, ut, seposita libertate eius, qua et ultro deus bonus, pro meritis cuiusque pensetur, dignis offeratur, indignis denegetur, ingratis auferatur, proinde omnibus aemulis uindicetur. ita omne hoc iustitiae opus procuratio bonitatis est: quod iudicando damnat, quod damnando punit, quod, ut dicitis. saeuit, utique bono, non malo proficit. denique timor iudicii ad bonum, non ad malum confert. non enim sufficiebat bonum per semetipsum commendari. iam sub aduersario laborans. nam et si commendabile per semetipsum, non tamen et conseruabile, quia expugnabile iam per aduersarium, nisi uis aliqua praeesset timendi, quae bonum etiam nolentes adpetere et custodire compelleret. ceterum tot inlecebris mali expugnantibus bonum quis illud appeteret, quod impune contemneret? quis custodiret quod sine periculo amitteret? legis mali uiam latam et multo frequentiorem: nonne omnes illa laberentur. si nihil in illa timeretur? horremus terribiles minas creatoris, et uix a malo auellimur. quid, si nihil minaretur? hanc iustitiam malum dices, quae malo non fauet? hanc bonum negabis, quae bono prospicit? qualem oportet deum uelles? qualem malis expediret? sub quo delicta gauderent? cui dia- , bolus inluderet? illum bonum iudicares deum, qui hominem posset magis malum facere securitate delicti? quis boni auctor, nisi qui et exactor? proinde quis mali extraneus, nisi qui et inimicus? quis inimicus, nisi qui et expugnator? quis expugnator, nisi qui et punitor? sic totus deus bonus est, dum pro bono omnia est. sic denique omnipotens, quia et iuuandi et laedendi potens. minus est tantummodo prodesse, quia non aliud quid possit quam prodesse. de eiusmodi qua fiducia bonum sperem, si hoc solum potest? quomodo innocentiae mercedem secter, si non et nocentiae spectem? diffidam necesse est, ne nec alteram partem remuneret qui utramque non ualuit. usque adeo iustitia etiam plenitudo est diuinitatis ipsius, exhibens deum perfectum, et patrem et dominum, patrem clementia dominum disciplina, patrem potestate blanda dominum seuera, patrem diligendum pie dominum timendum necessarie, diligendum, quia malit misericordiam quam sacrificium, et timendum. quia nolit peccatum, diligendum, quia malit paenitentiam peccatoris quam mortem, et timendum, quia nolit peccatores sui iam non paenitentes. ideo lex utrumque definit : diliges deum et: timebis deum. aliud obsecutori proposuit, aliud exorbitatori.
pass_a_gloss: For but so that evil afterwards erupted and from there now the goodness of God began to act with an adversary, also another task the same justice of God has found, now according to the adversary directing goodness, so that, having set aside its freedom, by which also God is good of his own accord, it may be weighed according to the merits of each, offered to the worthy, denied to the unworthy, taken away from the ungrateful, and thus avenged on all rivals. Thus all this work of justice is the management of goodness: what by judging it condemns, what by condemning it punishes, what, as you say, it rages, certainly profits the good, not the evil. Finally, the fear of judgment contributes to the good, not to the evil. For the good was not sufficient to be commended by itself. Now it labors under the adversary. For even if it is commendable by itself, it is not also preservable, because it is now expugnable by the adversary, unless some power of fear preceded, which would compel even the unwilling to seek and preserve the good. But with so many allures of evil expugning the good, who would seek it, which they could despise with impunity? Who would preserve it, which they could lose without danger? The way of evil is broad and much more frequented: would not all stumble upon it, if nothing were feared in it? We tremble at the terrible threats of the Creator, and we are hardly torn away from evil. What if nothing were threatened? You will say this justice is evil, which does not favor evil? You will deny this is good, which looks out for the good? What kind of God do you want? What kind would be expedient for evils? Under which sins would rejoice? To which the devil would mock? You would judge that God good, who could make man more evil with the security of sin? Who is the author of good, if not also the exactor? Thus who is extraneous to evil, if not also an enemy? Who is an enemy, if not also a conqueror? Who is a conqueror, if not also a punisher? So the whole God is good, while all things are for the good. So finally, omnipotent, because powerful both to help and to harm. It is less to benefit only, because it cannot do anything else than benefit. Of such a kind, with what confidence can I hope for good, if it can only do this? How can I seek the reward of innocence, if I do not also respect the punishment of guilt? I must distrust, lest the one who is not able to do both does not remunerate either part. So far justice is also the fullness of divinity itself, exhibiting God as perfect, and Father and Lord, Father with clemency, Lord with discipline, Father with gentle power, Lord with severe, Father to be loved piously, Lord to be feared necessarily, to be loved, because He prefers mercy to sacrifice, and to be feared, because He does not want sin, to be loved, because He prefers the repentance of the sinner to death, and to be feared, because He does not want His sinners, now not repentant. Therefore, the law defines both: you shall love God and: you shall fear God. It proposes one thing to the supplicant, another to the transgressor.

pass_b_english: When evil eventually erupted, God's goodness began to engage with an adversary, and God's justice took on a new task: to direct goodness in a way that counters the adversary. This means setting aside the freedom to act unilaterally, so that God's goodness can be weighed according to each person's merits, offered to those who are worthy, denied to those who are not, taken away from the ungrateful, and avenged on all rivals. The work of justice is essentially the management of goodness, condemning what is wrong, punishing what is condemned, and - as you put it - raging against evil, all of which ultimately serves the good, not the evil. The fear of judgment, in the end, contributes to the good, not the evil, because the good is not enough on its own to be commended. Now that it faces an adversary, the good is not just commendable, but also needs to be preserved, which it cannot be unless there is some power of fear to compel even the unwilling to seek and preserve it. With so many temptations of evil threatening the good, who would bother to seek it if they could despise it with impunity, or preserve it if they could lose it without danger? The way of evil is broad and well-trodden - wouldn't everyone stumble into it if there were nothing to fear? We tremble at the Creator's terrible threats, and yet we can barely tear ourselves away from evil. What if there were no threats? You would call this justice evil because it does not favor evil, and deny it is good because it looks out for the good. What kind of God do you want - one that would be useful to evil, under which sins would flourish, and at which the devil would mock? Would you consider a God who could make humans more evil by giving them a free pass to sin to be a good God? Who can be the author of good if not also the one who exacts it? Similarly, who can be extraneous to evil if not also its enemy, and who can be an enemy if not also a conqueror, and who can be a conqueror if not also a punisher? The whole of God is good because everything God does is for the good. This is what makes God omnipotent - powerful to both help and harm. To benefit only is less, because it means being unable to do anything else. With what confidence can I hope for good from a God who can only do good? How can I seek the reward of innocence if I do not also fear the punishment of guilt? I would have to distrust such a God, lest it fail to remunerate either the good or the evil. Justice is the fullness of divinity, exhibiting God as perfect, Father and Lord, a Father who is gentle and a Lord who disciplines, a Father to be loved and a Lord to be feared. We are to love God because God prefers mercy to sacrifice and fears sin, and to fear God because God prefers the repentance of sinners to death and does not want sinners who do not repent. The law makes this clear: we are to love God and fear God, with one approach for those who supplicate and another for those who transgress.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the relationship between God's goodness, justice, and the necessity of fear. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that preserves all nuances of agency and modality. The distinction between the 'supplicant' (obsecutori) and 'transgressor' (exorbitatori) is correctly handled. No scripture citations were present in the source text to verify.
